To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the order of the representational tools was more important than whether or not they matched to part-task demands; (2) teams receiving both tools performed better than teams that received only one tool; (3) teams receiving both mismatched tools performed better than those receiving both congruent tools; and (4) teams receiving both congruent and mismatched tools performed worse than teams receiving only one tool.

(a) providing learners with tools that support them in carrying out the part-task demands of specific problem phases, and (b) sequencing the tools in an order matched to the part-tasks, (c) resulted in better collaborative performance.

(1) teams receiving part-task matched tools constructed more task appropriate representations than teams receiving part-task mismatched tools and (2) teams receiving part task matched tools performed better on the learning-task than teams receiving part task mismatched tools.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of a tool that is suited for a specific part-task demand in the problem-solving process fosters learners’ qualitative and quantitative domain-reasoning and, thus, their collaborative performance on the complex learning task.
CSCL scripts should be tailored to the specific part-task demands of a learning-task, and should support learners’ collaborative construction of appropriate representations.
it is important to match the tools to the problem-solving process and to provide them in the right sequence.
